title.rendered: Nigeria needs stronger digital tax infrastructure — Taxaide

content.rendered:
The Chief Executive Officer of Taxaide Professional Services Limited, Bidemi Olumide, has urged the Federal Government to strengthen Nigeria’s digital tax infrastructure by deepening integration with private sector platforms to enable business scaling, improve data integrity and boost tax revenue.

Olumide made the call on 2 July while speaking at the opening of the 2026 National Tax Forum held at the University of Lagos.

He said the government must take the lead in building a digital tax ecosystem by opening its tax platforms through Application Programming Interfaces, allowing businesses to integrate their enterprise systems directly with government platforms.

Olumide said, “Government must lead the charge. The government is the one that creates the ecosystem. First, it makes sure that its platform is not just a platform-based data provision. Those platforms are extended as API interfaces. So, if I want to connect with REV360 today, the government should have created a programme to show what I need to do and the kind of APIs I need to have to connect with REV360 so that whatever information is needed from standard IT platforms can get directly to the government.”

He noted that fragmented data remained a major challenge to efficient tax administration, stressing that stronger integration will improve transparency and compliance.

“What we have today is that data is segregated. What you put in your system internally is different from what you’re going to find. That must stop. There must be data integrity. There must be API integration,” Olumide said.

The Taxaide CEO further stated that linking banking platforms with the tax system would broaden the tax base by incorporating more operators in the informal sector into the tax network.

He said, “The informal sector constitutes more than 55 per cent of our economy today, the largest in sub-Saharan Africa. With that singular integration between the banking system and the tax system, I think you’ve solved a lot of the problems of the informal sector largely. You’re able to track many more transactions.”

He added that businesses should be able to transmit payroll, invoicing and transaction data directly from their enterprise resource planning systems to government platforms.

“I would say that the state internal revenue service will file my payroll and pay your returns. Once I provide that information, the government sees it. If you come to my organisation, my hotel or my facility and I’m issuing you a receipt, that same ERP (software) is connected with the government. That is the fifth pillar that we must all come together with the government to build. Only the government can set the rules,” Olumide said.

He maintained that while the government had laid the foundation with platforms such as REV360, scaling digital tax administration would require active collaboration with the private sector.

“The infrastructure has been built by the government. The ecosystem requires every one of us. We cannot scale with just infrastructure. Government has to invite the private sector to drive technology adoption, using models already established in countries such as India, the United Kingdom and Brazil,” Olumide said.

The forum, themed ‘Nigeria’s New Tax Era: Implications for Businesses, the Informal Sector, and Revenue Performance,’ brought together government officials, tax administrators, academics, legal practitioners, economists and business leaders to examine the implementation of Nigeria’s newly enacted tax reforms and their implications for revenue mobilisation, investment and voluntary tax compliance.
